metaDescription: Only two true poultry shears fit this budget, Tingling and Jkrycyf. We compare steel, spring action, locks and what you give up versus pricier models.
introParagraphs: At the lowest budget tier for poultry shears, the field is small. We found just two distinct models that fit: the Tingling spring-loaded shears with 3.5mm 3Cr stainless steel blades, and the Jkrycyf spring-loaded shears in 3Cr13 stainless steel. Rather than pad the list with look-alike listings or ordinary scissors, this guide stays with those two and explains clearly what each one offers.

Both share the features that define a budget poultry shear: a spring-loaded assist that reopens the blades, a safety lock that keeps them closed in a drawer, and a heavy handle designed for gripping a bird. They differ on the details that matter when you actually cut: published blade thickness, handle material, and the extra functions the listings advertise. We evaluated both on those specifics.

What you give up at this tier is information and refinement. Neither listing advertises micro serrations, a take-apart pivot, or dishwasher approval, so cleaning after raw poultry is a hand-wash job. Spending more adds those features, and a higher tier is where blades that separate for cleaning appear. For an occasional roast chicken or a Thanksgiving turkey, though, the two shears here deliver the one thing that counts, which is a thick, spring-assisted blade.

products.name: Tingling Heavy Duty Poultry Shears
products.description:
The Tingling is the more clearly specified of the two. Its listing describes reinforced 3.5mm 3Cr stainless steel blades with a spring-loaded assist mechanism. That 3.5mm figure is the thickness often cited for poultry shears that work through joints and cartilage, which makes this the better-matched blade for spatchcocking.

A one-touch safety lock keeps the blades closed when stored, and the listing mentions 7cm blades that handle tasks like splitting lobster tails and trimming. The short blade length means you get leverage near the pivot, which is where force matters for bone, but it also means fewer long, clean slices through large cuts. The listing does not advertise serrations or a take-apart pivot.

In practice, the spring does the reopening, so you squeeze once per cut and let the handle return itself. That saves hand effort on a whole chicken, where you might cut a dozen times. Compared with the Jkrycyf, the Tingling publishes a thickness that the Jkrycyf does not, so it is the safer bet for bone and joint work. Check the product page for care instructions, because the listing text we evaluated does not state dishwasher approval.
products.bestFor: Home cooks who want published 3.5mm blades for spatchcocking at the lowest tier.
pros: Short blades give leverage near the pivot
cons: No take-apart pivot or serrations mentioned

products.name: Jkrycyf Spring Loaded Poultry Shears
products.description:
The Jkrycyf is the cheapest pick in the lineup, and it is built around 3Cr13 stainless steel blades that the listing says retain sharpness and resist rust. It uses a spring-loaded design with a safety lock, and the handles are ABS, described as comfortable and secure even when wet.

The listing positions it as a multi-purpose heavy duty shear for poultry, meat, herbs and vegetables, and it also mentions a bottle opener function. The maker does not publish a blade thickness, so you cannot assume it matches the Tingling's 3.5mm. The 3Cr13 label is a steel designation, not a thickness, and a spring plus a lock does not make a blade heavy enough for joints.

In use, the non-slip handle is the feature to appreciate when your hands are greasy from raw chicken. Compared with the Tingling, the Jkrycyf gives up a stated thickness in return for the lowest entry cost. It is the pick for someone who cuts chicken parts and trims fat a few times a year, not for someone who spatchcocks every weekend.
products.bestFor: Occasional cooks who want a spring-loaded, locking shear at the lowest cost.
pros: ABS handle is non-slip even when wet
cons: No take-apart pivot or serrations mentioned

buyingCriteria.explanation: Poultry shears are often around 3.5mm, because thinner blades flex against cartilage and joints. Of the two picks here, only the Tingling publishes a figure, 3.5mm, and the Jkrycyf does not. A missing number is not proof of weakness, but it means you cannot verify strength before you buy. If spatchcocking is your goal, favor the pick that states its thickness.

A spring reopens the blades after each cut, so you squeeze once and the handle returns. Both listings describe a spring-loaded design. That reduces hand effort over a whole bird. Some spring designs can lock up if squeezed fully closed, so check how the mechanism behaves near the end of the cut.

A lock keeps the blades closed in a drawer, which protects fingers and the edge. The Tingling lists a one-touch safety lock and the Jkrycyf lists a safety lock too. Test the lock a few times after unboxing, because a lock that is stiff or loose affects how you use the shear daily. Always engage the lock before putting the shear back in a drawer.

Greasy hands from raw poultry make a slick handle risky. The Jkrycyf lists ABS handles described as non-slip even when wet. The Tingling listing does not specify a handle material in the excerpt we evaluated. If slipperiness worries you, favor the pick with the stated grip and wipe your hands before the cut.

Raw poultry can leave residue at the pivot, so ease of cleaning matters. Neither listing advertises a take-apart pivot or dishwasher approval. You will need to wash by hand with hot soapy water, open the blades fully and dry them thoroughly before storing. Take-apart designs appear at a higher tier.

Both listings use common stainless grades: 3Cr for the Tingling and 3Cr13 for the Jkrycyf. These steels can be sharpened with a wet stone, and very soft steel dulls fast. Dry the blades after washing, because moisture is the usual cause of rust on budget stainless. Do not use either one for hard bones such as beef ribs.

howWeEvaluated.title: Blade evidence
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated thickness and steel designation. The Tingling states 3.5mm 3Cr stainless steel and the Jkrycyf states 3Cr13 stainless steel with no thickness. We scored an unpublished thickness as unknown, not as weak.

howWeEvaluated.title: Mechanism and safety
howWeEvaluated.description: Both picks list a spring-loaded design and a safety lock. We looked at how each listing describes the lock and the assist, and we noted that the Tingling calls its lock a one-touch design.

howWeEvaluated.title: Grip
howWeEvaluated.description: The Jkrycyf lists ABS non-slip handles for wet hands. The Tingling listing in our research does not specify handle material. Grip was weighted heavily because raw poultry is slippery.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cleaning access
howWeEvaluated.description: Neither listing advertises take-apart or dishwasher use. We treated both as hand-wash tools and noted that this is the main thing a higher tier adds.

howWeEvaluated.title: Lineup positioning
howWeEvaluated.description: The Tingling leads on published thickness and the one-touch lock. The Jkrycyf leads on lowest entry cost, wet-hand grip and the bottle opener function. We evaluated specs and buyer feedback in broad terms and did not claim hands-on testing.

faq.q: Which of the two should I buy for spatchcocking?
faq.a: The Tingling, because it publishes 3.5mm blades, the thickness often cited for poultry shears. The Jkrycyf states a steel grade but no thickness. If you spatchcock regularly, that evidence is worth the difference.

faq.q: Why are there only two picks?
faq.a: Only two distinct poultry-shear models fit this budget in our research. We left out duplicates, color variants and ordinary scissors rather than pad the list. If you want more choices, the next price tier has several more models.

Neither listing we evaluated advertises dishwasher approval. Check the product page, and treat both as hand-wash tools. Open the blades fully, scrub the pivot with hot soapy water and dry them before storing.

faq.q: Do spring-loaded shears have any downside?
faq.a: Some spring designs can lock up if squeezed fully closed, and a spring adds a part that can wear. The benefit is less hand effort over many cuts. Both picks here use a spring, so test the action when you first use them.
They are designed for poultry bones and joints, but not for hard bones such as beef ribs. Cutting hard bone will chip or bend the blade. Use the shears near joints, and avoid twisting while cutting.
Higher tiers add serrated blades, take-apart pivots and dishwasher approval. Those features help with grip and cleaning, not just cutting. For occasional use, the two shears here are enough.
